{{short description|Bitcoin's ability to handle transaction volume}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2017}}
{{broader|Bitcoin}}
[[File:Bitcoin over Lightning Network.svg|thumb|350x350px|The [[Lightning Network]] is a secondary network designed to address bitcoin scalability]]

'''Bitcoin scalability''' refers to the capability of the [[Bitcoin]] network to handle large amounts of transaction data on its platform.<ref>[The Limits to Blockchain? Scaling vs. Decentralization.] Social Science Research Network. ''Cybersecurity, Privacy & Networks eJournal.'' Accessed 21 April 2019.</ref> Records (known as ''blocks'') in the Bitcoin [[Bitcoin#Blockchain|blockchain]] are limited in size and frequency to prioritize security and decentralization by keeping the cost of running a Bitcoin node affordable.<ref name="onscaling" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bier |first=Jonathan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mjNizgEACAAJ |title=The Blocksize War |date=2021-03-11 |publisher=Independently Published |isbn=979-8-7107-4951-7 |language=en}}</ref> With an average block creation time of 10 minutes and a block size limit of around 1 megabyte, the base layer processes an estimated 3.3 to 7 transactions per second.<ref name="mastering">{{cite book |first=Andreas M. | last=Antonopoulos |date=April 2014 |isbn=978-1-4493-7404-4 |publisher=O'Reilly Media |title=Mastering Bitcoin. Unlocking Digital Crypto-Currencies}}</ref>{{rp|ch. 2}}<ref name="onscaling">{{cite book |last1=Croman |first1=Kyle |title=Financial Cryptography and Data Security |last2=Eyal |first2=Ittay |date=2016 |chapter=On Scaling Decentralized Blockchains |chapter-url=http://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~prateeks/papers/Bitcoin-scaling.pdf |volume= 9604|pages= 106–125|doi=10.1007/978-3-662-53357-4_8 |access-date=10 December 2017 | quote=The maximum throughput is the maximum rate at which the blockchain can confirm transactions. Today, bitcoin’s maximum throughput is 3.3–7 transactions/sec [1]. This number is constrained by the maximum block size and the inter-block time.|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |isbn=978-3-662-53356-7 }}</ref>

Scalability is often contrasted with [[Computer security|security]] and [[decentralization]].<ref name=":0" />  

The term "Layer 2" is used for systems, such as the [[Lightning Network]], which process multiple transactions more quickly using a separate network and then updating the bitcoin blockchain in batches.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hijfte |first=Stijn Van |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IivxDwAAQBAJ |title=Blockchain Platforms: A Look at the Underbelly of Distributed Platforms |date=2020-07-06 |publisher=Morgan & Claypool Publishers |isbn=978-1-68173-892-5 |language=en}}</ref>

==Background==
The block size limit, and the proof-of-work difficulty adjustment settings of bitcoin's consensus protocol, creates a [[Bottleneck (production)|bottleneck]] in bitcoin's transaction processing capacity. This can result in increased transaction fees and delayed processing of transactions that cannot be fit into a block.<ref name="hopesto">{{Cite news |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/bitcoin-unlimited-hopes-to-save-bitcoin-from-itself-block-size/ |title='Bitcoin Unlimited' Hopes to Save Bitcoin from Itself |first=Jordan | last=Pearson |access-date=17 January 2017 |date=14 October 2016 |work=Motherboard |publisher=Vice Media LLC }}</ref> Proposals for how to scale bitcoin have lead to contentious debate. ''[[Business Insider]]'' in 2017 characterized this debate as an "ideological battle over bitcoin's future."<ref name="businessinsider20170326">{{Cite news |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/bitcoins-hard-fork-bitcoin-unlimited-segregated-witness-explained-2017-3 |title=A Bitcoin civil war is threatening to tear the digital currency in 2 — here's what you need to know |first1=Oscar | last1=Williams-Grut | first2=Rob | last2=Price |access-date=2 July 2017 |date=26 March 2017 |work=Business Insider }}</ref>

==Efficiency improvements==
Technical optimizations may decrease the amount of computing resources required to receive, process and record bitcoin transactions, allowing increased throughput without placing extra demand on the bitcoin network. These modifications can be to either the network, in which case a fork is required, or to individual node software (such as [[Bitcoin Core]]).
* [[Schnorr signature]]s have been proposed as a scaling system by [[Blockstream]] co-founder Pieter Wuille.
* A 2006 paper by [[Mihir Bellare]] enables signature aggregation in O(1) size, which means that it will not take more space to have multiple signers. Bellare-Neven reduces to Schnorr for a single key.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/kanzure/diyhpluswiki/blob/master/transcripts/bitcoin-core-dev-tech/2017-09-06-signature-aggregation.mdwn|title=kanzure/diyhpluswiki|website=GitHub|date=9 October 2021}}</ref> Bellare-Neven has been implemented.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/461|title = &#91;WIP&#93; Aggregate signature module implementation by apoelstra · Pull Request #461 · bitcoin-core/Secp256k1| website=[[GitHub]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference|title=Multi-Signatures in the Plain Public-Key Model and a General Forking Lemma|author=Mihir Bellare and Gregory Neven|book-title=Proceedings of the 13th ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS 2006)|pages=390–399|year=2006|publisher=ACM|url=https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~mihir/papers/multisignatures.pdf|access-date=2025-10-14|quote=A multi-signature scheme enables a group of signers to produce a compact, joint signature on a common document, and has many potential uses. ... Our multi-signature schemes achieve signature aggregation with constant-size signatures (O(1)), and the security is provably reduced to the standard Discrete Logarithm problem (i.e., Schnorr in the single-key case).}}</ref>{{primary source inline|date=August 2026}}

==Additional systems==
{{See also |Lightning Network}}

[[File:Lightning Network Explained.webm|thumb|A Lightning Network overview]]

The [[Lightning Network]] (LN) is a protocol that aims to improve bitcoin's scalability and speed.<ref name="MasteringBitcoin">{{cite book |last1=Antonopoulos |first1=Andreas |title=Mastering Bitcoin |publisher=O'Reilly |isbn=978-1491954386 |pages=297–304 |edition=2nd |year=2017 }}</ref>

In January 2018 [[Blockstream]] launched a payment processing system for web retailers called "Lightning Charge", noted that lightning was live on mainnet with 200 nodes operating as of 27 January 2018 and advised it should still be considered "in testing". The Liquid Network is a sidechain that Blockstream developed which is built on top of Bitcoin.<ref>{{Cite news |title=New Crypto Consortium Seeks to Alleviate Liquidity Problems |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-10-10/new-crypto-consortium-seeks-to-alleviate-liquidity-problems |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181227084723/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-10-10/new-crypto-consortium-seeks-to-alleviate-liquidity-problems |archive-date=2018-12-27 |access-date=2026-04-29 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>  It processes blocks every minute instead of every 10 minutes.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hijfte |first=Stijn Van |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IivxDwAAQBAJ |title=Blockchain Platforms: A Look at the Underbelly of Distributed Platforms |date=2020-07-06 |publisher=Morgan & Claypool Publishers |isbn=978-1-68173-892-5 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=New Crypto Consortium Seeks to Alleviate Liquidity Problems |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-10-10/new-crypto-consortium-seeks-to-alleviate-liquidity-problems |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181227084723/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-10-10/new-crypto-consortium-seeks-to-alleviate-liquidity-problems |archive-date=2018-12-27 |access-date=2026-04-29 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref>

As part of a government program to expand the use of [[Bitcoin in El Salvador]], the El Salvador introduced a wallet based on the Lightning Network protocol while allowing for other Bitcoin Lightning wallets.  The government distributed {{Currency|30|USD}} in bitcoin to people who sign up to use an electronic wallet called "Chivo".<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Pérez|first1=Santiago|last2=Ostroff|first2=Caitlin|date=August 26, 2021|title=El Salvador Gets Ready for a Risky Bitcoin Experiment|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/el-salvador-gets-ready-for-a-risky-bitcoin-experiment-11629966845|url-access=subscription|access-date=August 26, 2021}}</ref> Chivo was run by a private enterprise, but information regarding the platform and its policies were classified by the government.<ref name="Kurmanaev-2021">{{Cite news|last1=Kurmanaev|first1=Anatoly|last2=Avelar|first2=Bryan|last3=Livni|first3=Ephrat|date=2021-10-07|title=Bitcoin Preaches Financial Liberty. A Strongman Is Testing That Promise.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/07/world/americas/bitcoin-el-salvador-bukele.html|access-date=2022-01-27|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> <ref>{{Cite web|title=Countries That Defied Odds in Terms of Crypto Acceptance|work=Urban Kenyans|date=9 November 2022|url=https://urbankenyans.com/countries-that-defied-odds-in-terms-of-crypto-acceptance/|access-date=12 November 2022|archive-date=4 October 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004022019/https://urbankenyans.com/countries-that-defied-odds-in-terms-of-crypto-acceptance/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In December, 2024, El Salvador, in an agreement for a $1.4 billion loan from the [[International Monetary Fund|IMF]], the government began to wind-down its involvement in the Chivo wallet.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pérez |first=Santiago |title=El Salvador Made Bitcoin an Official Currency. Now It's Backtracking for IMF Loan. |url=https://www.wsj.com/world/americas/el-salvador-made-bitcoin-an-official-currency-now-its-backtracking-for-imf-loan-874c6623 |access-date=2024-12-19 |website=WSJ |date=18 December 2024 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Renteria |first=Nelson |date=2024-12-19 |title=El Salvador says it will keep buying bitcoin despite IMF warning |url=https://www.reuters.com/markets/currencies/el-salvadors-bitcoin-wallet-be-sold-or-discontinued-after-deal-with-imf-official-2024-12-19/ |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

==Block size increases==
Bitcoin's transaction throughput is limited by two parameters:
* the ''block time'' determines how often a new block is added to the chain,
* the ''block size'' determines the amount of data that can be added with every block.

Bitcoin has a block time of 10 minutes and a block size of 1 MB. Various increases to this limit, and proposals to remove it completely, have been proposed over bitcoin's history. Implementing any of these proposals involves a [[Fork (blockchain)|fork]]. The common argument against such increases is the additional difficulty and expense of running a full node (i.e. one carrying the entire [[distributed ledger]]). This is due to the increased overall size of the ledger<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Heo |first1=Jun Wook |last2=Ramachandran |first2=Gowri Sankar |last3=Dorri |first3=Ali |last4=Jurdak |first4=Raja |date=2024-07-31 |title=Blockchain Data Storage Optimisations: A Comprehensive Survey |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3645104 |journal=ACM Computing Surveys |language=en |volume=56 |issue=7 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1145/3645104 |issn=0360-0300|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref>, which puts puts pressure on the node in terms of both [[Random-access memory|RAM]] and [[Computer data storage|storage space]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Huan |last2=Wang |first2=Yijie |date=September 2020 |title=MiniChain: A lightweight protocol to combat the UTXO growth in public blockchain |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0743731520302732 |journal=Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing |language=en-US |volume=143 |pages=67–76 |doi=10.1016/j.jpdc.2020.05.001 |issn=0743-7315 |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20230810083454/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0743731520302732 |archive-date=2023-08-10|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[Litecoin]] produces blocks four times faster than Bitcoin which leads to a 4x improvement in throughput. [[Dogecoin]] has even more throughput with a block time of 1 minute. [[Bitcoin Cash]] has a block size of 32 MB and hence 32x more throughput than Bitcoin. [[Bitcoin SV]] removed the block size limit altogether.

===Proposed===
* [[Bitcoin XT]] was proposed in 2015 to increase the transaction processing capacity of bitcoin by increasing the block size limit.<ref name="Hern-2015">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2015/aug/17/bitcoin-xt-alternative-cryptocurrency-chief-scientist|title=Bitcoin's forked: chief scientist launches alternative proposal for the currency|author=Alex Hern|work=the Guardian|date=17 August 2015|access-date=20 August 2015}}</ref>
* [[Bitcoin Classic]] was proposed in 2016 to increase the transaction processing capacity of bitcoin by increasing the block size limit.
* "The Hong Kong Agreement" was a 2016 agreement of some miners and developers that contained a timetable that would see both the activation of the Segregated Witness ([[SegWit]]) proposal established in December 2015 by Bitcoin Core developers, and the development of a block size limit increased to 2 MB. However, both timelines were missed.
* SegWit2x was a proposed hard fork of the cryptocurrency bitcoin. The implementation of Segregated Witness in August 2017 was only the first half of the so-called "New York Agreement" by which those who wanted to increase effective block size by SegWit compromised with those who wanted to increase block size by a hard fork to a larger block size.<ref>{{cite news | last = Vigna | first = Paul | title = Bitcoin Dodges Split That Threatened Its Surging Price | newspaper = [[The Wall Street Journal]] | date = 8 November 2017 | url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/bitcoin-dodges-split-that-threatened-its-surging-price-1510172701/ | access-date = 8 November 2017 | archive-date = 8 November 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171108204840/https://www.wsj.com/articles/bitcoin-dodges-split-that-threatened-its-surging-price-1510172701 | url-status = dead }}</ref>  The second half of SegWit2x involved a hard fork in November 2017 to increase the blocksize to 2 megabytes. On 8 November 2017 the developers of SegWit2x announced that the hard fork planned for around 16 November 2017 was canceled for the time being due to a lack of consensus.
* [[Bitcoin Unlimited]] advocated for miner flexibility to increase the block size limit. This proposal is different from Bitcoin Core in that the block size parameter is not hard-coded, and rather the nodes and miners flag support for the size that they want, using an idea they refer to as 'emergent consensus'.
